sections.body_md:
Writing the differential equation is the second step. The first step is deciding what the model is for. A control model is not a catalog of every effect you can name. It is the smallest description that still gets the loop's behavior right: the right stored quantities, the right units, and the right split between fast effects you can collapse and slow effects you must keep.

A state is a stored quantity that needs an initial condition: position of a mass, charge on a capacitor, level in a tank. A command, a reference, and a disturbance are inputs unless you give them dynamics of their own.

Units catch algebra errors before any simulation does. Scaling then turns the surviving terms into pure numbers, so a coefficient of 0.01 can be compared with a coefficient of 1 and dropped on purpose.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
A time scale from a length \(L\) and a velocity \(V\) is \(L/V\). A rotational speed in revolutions per minute becomes radians per second by
\[
\omega = N_{\mathrm{rpm}} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{60}.
\]
A sensor gain converts the measured unit into the signal unit by multiplication, not by addition. Force is mass times acceleration. At a resting point every derivative is zero, which is an algebraic equation for the state. A ratio of a slow time scale to a fast one tells you whether the fast piece can be replaced by the gain it settles to.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A tank level is read over a depth of 150 mm, which is 0.15 m. The flow you care about moves that surface at about 0.01 m/s, so the level time scale is \(0.15/0.01 = 15\) s. The valve that sets the flow moves in 0.05 s. The ratio of those scales is \(15/0.05 = 300\). A level loop over tens of seconds can treat the valve as an immediate gain. Entering 150 mm as 150 m would make the time scale 15000 s and send the design after the wrong plant.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Calling an input a state, or a state an input, swaps the columns of the model you write next. Comparing terms that still carry different units will drop the wrong one. A loop that is required to have zero steady error needs the integrator that produces that fact; a model that omits it will predict an error the hardware will not show. The halfway point of a measured step is not the time constant. For one real pole, the time constant is the 63% time.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Linearization builds a local linear model at the resting point you just solved. Identification reads a time constant and a gain back out of a measured step. Equilibrium calculations are the same derivative-equals-zero step, done for a plant you intend to hold.
